text: The length of the menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. A typical cycle is between 21 and 35 days, and periods usually start between the ages of 10 and 16. It can take up to 2 years after a first period for cycles to become regular.

Heavy menstrual bleeding is when you need to change a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, or you pass clots larger than about 2.5 cm. See a GP if heavy bleeding affects your daily life, you pass large clots, or you bleed between periods or after sex.

Periods are irregular if they come more often than every 21 days or less often than every 35 days, or if the length of your cycle changes by 7 days or more between periods. Common causes include stress, weight changes, and conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome. A GP can assess you and run tests if needed.

Normal menstrual flow can last between 2 and 7 days, and the average amount of blood lost during a period is about 60 milliliters. Missing periods can be caused by pregnancy, but also by stress, low body weight, excessive exercise, and hormonal conditions. A health care provider can help determine the cause.

If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself or of not wanting to live, this is a medical emergency. Reach out to a trusted person immediately, contact local emergency services, or call a crisis support line in your country. You do not have to face this alone.

PMS is a collection of physical and emotional symptoms that happen in the days before a period starts, such as bloating, breast tenderness, mood changes, and tiredness. Symptoms usually stop once the period begins. Self-care measures and pain relief available from pharmacies may help; a GP can advise if symptoms are severe.
